entities.summary:
Lando, whose pontificate lasted from July 913 to March 914, served as Pope during one of the most tumultuous and obscure periods in papal history, often termed the Saeculum obscurum (the "Dark Age" of the Papacy, 904–964). His brief reign of approximately seven months epitomized the profound political weakness of the Holy See and the overwhelming dominance of the Roman aristocracy, particularly the powerful Theophylacti family. Elevated from an unknown background, Lando's pontificate was less a period of independent ecclesiastical governance and more a reflection of the intense, often violent, power struggles among competing Roman factions, with the papacy itself becoming a prize rather than a moral authority.

During Lando's brief tenure, no significant ecclesiastical reforms, doctrinal pronouncements, or major political interventions are recorded. His election itself was a product of the prevailing aristocratic control, following the similarly short and uneventful pontificate of Anastasius III. The real power in Rome was wielded by figures like Theophylact I, the Vestarius and Consul of Rome, and his wife Theodora, who effectively dictated papal succession and policy. Lando's pontificate thus passed largely without distinct events, serving primarily as a placeholder between more influential or notorious figures, with the Roman See effectively a pawn in the hands of secular magnates.
